371.t: Producers, concepts and having a 'point of view' on records
371.s: Jones values producers as idea men; recording projects work best with a theme and ideas usually come from the producer.
371.q: I think it's critical. They are like, I guess you can call them idea men. They come up with the ideas that keep the company afloat. If it weren’t for people like that, no one would have the various suggestions for putting various artists together are doing a special type of project with a special…

371.t: Declining to discuss a date with a mystic bandleader
371.s: Jones refuses comment on a record date with a mystic, saying only that the checks arrived on time.
371.q: Don’t quote me. (Laughs) I mean…Next! The only good thing about that date was that the checks came in on time. I’ll say no more. . So that's why I don't want to say anything. I don't want to say anything that would impact on somebody's credibility. That is why don't want to comment on it.

371.t: GG Grice and the Donald Byrd jazz lab group; record dates with unknown labels
371.s: Jones was never in the lab group but recorded with Grice; recording names were often invented later, and musicians rarely knew who paid.
371.q: I don't know that much about it, but their name suggests, at least to me, that they did a bunch of experimental playing. It probably wasn't down the middle, straight-line jazz, but little excursions. It was that kind of stuff. It was something like what they do today that is called avant-garde…

509.s: She calls Steeplechase crooks who owe her money, praises Perception, and notes Mercury pushing her to stand.
509.q: They were crooks, Steeplechase, right today. They owe me money. It‘s kind of a joke now. It‘s been . . . I don‘t know how many years it was I recorded with them, but it was my first time to the North Sea, I think it was, and they recorded three albums during that time. They‘ve messed over so many…

509.t: Fights with Richard Seidel over producer credit
509.s: She produces herself and refused to let Seidel take producer credit, even after he flew to California.
509.q: Hell no, I produce my own stuff, you know. And Richard Seidel, oh, man. He thinks he discovered me. And I looked at him, I said, ―You‘re such a silly little boy. I‘m dealing with little boys here.‖ It‘s all about him getting his name on as producer. And the first couple of times I didn‘t pay…

509.t: Recording for Perception Records and Johnny Pate
509.s: While home she made Where Are You Going? for a Chicago label, Perception, dedicated to her daughter.
509.ch: Staying home, image and being a woman leader
509.q: No, that wasn‘t Steeplechase then. That was . . . it was something called . . . see, I was home. I was doing Perception.

64.t: Why he moved from label to label and managers
64.s: He argues record companies did not know how to market piano leaders, and envied only Garner and Evans for having managers.
64.q: It was difficult in those days for people to conceive of a piano leader in the context of making a lot of money. If you were Dave Ruebeck and you broke through with a hot record okay. If you were Earl Garner and you broke through with a hot record, okay. But you have to realize that those were two…

64.t: Ahmad Jamal, the Chess brothers and Ramsey Lewis
64.s: He explains how Chess promoted Jamal and Ramsey Lewis as piano leaders through their radio network and what happened to others.
64.q: No. It did not. [Unintelligible] Jamal should be one of the people who is recognized according to his influence. I mean he is one of the most influential pianist of the 50’s or that particular period in his life. And the only reason his influence has not continued on the same level is because he…

64.t: Blue Note, merchandising and hustling his own gigs
64.s: His business knowledge worried labels, Blue Note neglected several pianists, and he decided to rely on clubs rather than record companies.
64.q: Yeah. It became very apparent, very early in my career that you couldn’t do, and I don’t say this to put anybody down at Bluenote but Bluenote had a way of handling musicians, which I didn’t see eye to eye with. I mean I love what they did. I love what they did with Hart Silver and Herbie Hancock…

382.t: Poor distribution of the Andy Razaf album and the label owner
382.s: About two hundred albums were pressed and nothing came of it; she likes 'Mound Bayou' and 'Massachusetts'.
382.ch: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
382.q: Well now you see Leonard Feather, he had access to some of these, I guess to this little company Period Records and they weren't even doing pop music. I mean they were doing classical music. And it started when he got the Kirby Group together, you know, and they called up Flow Down Gently, "Sweet…

382.t: The Andy Razaf tribute album on Period
382.s: She discusses the album for Andy Razaf, Leonard Feather's idea, missing tracks in the discography, its low-budget release, and hopes for reissue.
382.q: Well, as a result of the earlier session for Period Records, Leonard got in touch with me and suggested that we do a tribute to Andy Razaf.

382.t: Rights, consignment and artists selling their own albums
382.s: How the festival recordings' rights are given up, flat fees, and artists selling albums themselves.
382.q: Yes. Of course, today with the industry like it is, these things would probably never get any further than the box. It makes the producer and the performer pretty independent of each other, and at the same time, it's an opportunity for the performer to, let' say, benefit by performing; because he…

189.t: Distribution failure and losing about ten thousand dollars
189.s: Airplay on WYLD, but pressing plant delays killed sales; he lost close to ten thousand dollars.
189.q: No. See, I wasn't thinking about it. I just said, this is good material. I thought if you just make something with good material, the public ahead won the radio. Now, W.Y.L.D. played it a lot.

189.s: He ran Pontchartrain, lost his copies, arranged Don't Make No Noise.
189.q: And about the Internal Revenue? Mm-hmm. Internal Revenue, that's on there, too. I know I recorded it. Yeah, you can't beat Uncle Sam.

121.t: Spreading Life and remixing Live While You Can
121.s: Eddie Bo talked Ridgley into funding a label for a tune already cut; Ridgley remixed the Live While You Can master from Mrs. Walker's tape with Allen Toussaint's help.

121.s: Joe Assunto's One Stop record; Eddie Bo's funky I Want Some Money was changed by Wardell's arrangement; London did not promote it, recorded at Cosmo.

And Eddie Bo wrote this, I Want Some Money. Now this is, we're going to talk about this. This is interesting. I Want…

289.t: Buying acts and recording Irma Thomas and Chris Kenner
289.s: After Slim he bought acts from agencies, adding band and commission; he recorded only Slim, Irma Thomas and Chris Kenner.
289.q: Well, after Slim, well after Slim, we started buying acts, you know. Yeah. Buying acts for five nights. And of course, you can look on the wall and see some of these. Yeah. Oh yeah. We started buying acts. And then later down the line, I told you, I record this girl, I'm a termist.

289.t: Moving Slim to Specialty through Johnny Vincent
289.s: Because the small label's publishing and distribution were weak, Stovall took Slim to Specialty via Johnny Vincent, and the records took off.
289.q: It really took off. People knew who he was, you know, and he was behind it. So this guy didn't have any money, and his publishing wasn't right. Everything behind him was all together wrong. It wasn't out he was trying to steal, but he just didn't have the set out. So I told Slim, I said, now the…

780.t: Session run by someone else; Don Robey holds back release
780.s: He recalls who ran the Peacock session and says Don Robey delayed release until he recovered, which never came.
780.q: No, uh, no. He didn't play. He didn't play anything, I don't think. Uh, well he could, but uh, he didn't. You know, he could play, you know, I think he, he played piano. And his wife, uh, she sung. And he was in charge of the session.

780.t: Dave Bartholomew's demand for half and Imperial's dominance
780.s: Bartholomew required his name on records released on Imperial, the biggest New Orleans label.
780.q: Dave was out of his hands on it? Dave was out of his hands on everything that was released on Imperial. Everybody records for Imperial. Dave wouldn't record it unless you put your name on it.

958.t: No label pressure at Sony and being a banjo player on a major
958.s: Fleck is surprised Sony has not pressured them despite modest sales. He found it cool to be an esoteric group on a major label, like Earl Scruggs before him.
958.q: I don’t understand why I’m not getting that pressure. I mean we’re on SONY, they’re spending this big money. Our sales haven’t been that great. They have not put the phone down. Maybe it’s because we’re near the end of the deal and they want to re-sign us, I don’t know. But no, I’ve been very…

958.t: Music reshaped by producers and the value of artistic control
958.s: Fleck explains that music can be shaped by producers or executives chasing hits. Producing and recording at home gives artistic control, and he sees no motive to sell out.
958.q: Well I guess I was talking about feeling the hand of somebody — once it gets recorded that’s what it is. But sometimes by the time it gets recorded it’s been shaped by hands other than the artists, and I think that’s what I was talking about. Like for instance if the Flecktones had come up with…

962.t: Producers pressing her to change her approach
962.s: Early in her career producers pushed commercial changes; now she simply states her position.
962.q: Um hum. That’s happened. Yeah. That happened early on in my career. And not so much now. Once in a while, I’ve had a producer to try that on. But that was a very short conversation you know without even getting — I didn’t even have to get angry about it or even concerned. I just stated where I was…

962.s: Producers often disagree on which originals to include; she respects them but sometimes insists.
962.q: All the time, yeah. That’s all the time. There’s no animosity involved, it’s just kind of a “yeah, no.” That’s it. And you know, and I trust my producers. I’ve worked with several over the years and I trust and respect them all. And then sometimes it comes to, “No, I want that one. That one stays,…

1002.t: Independent revolution and learning the record business
1002.s: Owning the label meant no one else to blame; they learned radio, promotion and distribution around the dining room table.
1002.q: Right. Right. So we worked 24 hours — we were so excited I think that the new adventure, the autonomy gave us so much energy, being on our own and to make it happen. So we would lose a lot of sleep thinking about how we were going to do things. Because we didn’t know how to do things. We learned,…

1002.t: Selling Tribe records worldwide and licensing from 1990
1002.s: First markets were Poland and the Czech Republic; Harrison sold boxes to distributors, chased late payments, then licensed masters abroad from 1990.
1002.q: The first big marketplace we hit was Poland. Poland. The Czech Republic. You know they’re the ones that did the big write-up in a magazine talking about the label and talking about the first three different releases and whatnot. Then Germany, then France and Spain and eventually Japan, Australia…

808.s: She dislikes promoting herself; Frishberg and Dan Barrett led her to Arbors and jazz parties; Rowe reads a review.
808.q: Pretty much but I’m not very good at it. It’s very hard if you’re insecure to kind of try to sell yourself. So I just try to work on the music and hope that things sell themselves. And I’ve been extremely lucky in my relationship with Dave Frishberg, he was an Arbors recording artist and he got me…

808.t: Arbors terms, CD sales, and the March of Jazz
808.s: Arbors pays for sessions and sells her CDs at a discount; the label is supportive and runs the March of Jazz festival.
808.q: Well I purchase them for my local gigs. They have distributors who stock the stores in our areas so I don’t have to worry about that. But I can sell as many as I want on gigs and to friends and stuff. And so I can make a little profit on that which is nice.

443.t: Difficulty getting recorded: Concord, Jazzology, Nagel Heyer
443.s: Concord never recorded him; Jazzology recorded him via Phil Carroll's Atlanta party, and he made Nagel Heyer discs in Germany, including with Terry Blaine.

443.s: He works out the cost of producing a CD and the sales he expects at concerts.

141.t: Leaving Atlantic in 1980 and Bruce Lundvall at Elektra-Musician
141.s: He left over an advance dispute and signed with Lundvall, who never told him what to do.
141.q: No. I liked Bruce Lundvall, and... He was a fan of mine way before...when I made “Baby, Please Don’t Go” on Columbia. He became a fan with that, and he’d listened to that several times.

372.t: Atlantic contract and the 'Confucius' restaurant record
372.s: He recalls the Tristano date with Art Taylor and Gene Ramey, his discomfort, and the late release.

374.ch: Later years: recordings, Alice and the book
374.q: For one thing, Giovanni actually rescued American music, because no other companies were going for jazz. So he came in, and you have to give him credit for saving the music, because people, jazz was the last thing they thought of. But still . . .

4.t: Los Angeles record companies of the late 1940s and what Spikes missed
4.s: Willard raises the Exclusive label and War Perkins; Spikes says he lacked promotion savvy, never gave bands professional copies, and might have become a millionaire.
4.ch: Shows, scripts and the Mosby-era names

4.t: Ray Rovin and the short-lived Music Town record company

380.t: Red Records and the Modern masters

380.s: He and Buddy Collette, Al Aarons and others started Legend, which fell apart when a partner dipped into the petty cash.

90.t: Other labels and the honking show-business routine

385.s: Producers pick musicians who do not mix, then blame the leader when records fail.

385.q: fellas that don't mix. . . . Not that they can't play they just don't mix. And they would do that type of thing and it didn't come out right. And they produce and then . . . if the record didn't sell, then they blame it on you, when he did all the pickin' and the songs and everything.

385.t: Television with Frankie Lymon; Profound Blues with Houston Person
385.s: Gotham got him on TV, and he says producers hire the sidemen and name the tunes but blame the leader.

412.t: Plain Old Blues, small labels and the business of music

412.ch: Chicago in the 1950s: Mercury, unions and jobbing
412.q: I found this is the business music, as opposed to the business of playing music. This is the business music. And most musicians don't care for the business of music, and you can see why. There's a thing I never heard of. I'm now a talent scout. If they had paid me for bringing them that tune, it…

454.t: Record companies hiding that jazz sells
454.s: Festival crowds versus what record companies admit; jazz sells again and again and costs less to make than rock.
454.ch: Massey Hall, race and the record business
454.q: The record companies. I feel that not only my music, but Duke's music, by most -- even the big record companies, that they try and make jazz like it doesn't sell.

454.t: Breaking the bootleggers and the record business

74.t: Sonora records and the mix of singing and solos

279.t: Reviews, the Capitol session and Barry Ulanov

66.t: Moe Asch's love of artists, and bringing Erroll Garner and Art Tatum to him
66.s: Asch let artists record whatever they wanted. She brought in Erroll Garner and Art Tatum, who recorded for little money, and she took Asch's recordings to Pittsburgh.
66.ch: Cafe Society and the Zodiac Suite
66.q: Yes, it was different because Moe Ash had more love and he had more respect for jazz artists. Often he would take us to dinner, the nicest dinners, steak dinners, the nicest places and it was his idea that an artist should be heard if they're talented. He'd turn the tape on and go away, let you…

67.t: How little records mattered to bands and bookings
67.s: Records were unpopular until Armstrong's Hot Five; Mamie Smith and Johnny Dunn sold best, and recording paid little and did not bring bookings.
67.ch: Chicago clubs, entertainers and tent shows
67.q: Well they weren't too popular in those days. Recording was just -- it was hard to get a recording, because they weren't buying records in those days, other than say Mame Smith records. Mame Smith I think sold more records than any of the singers. During that time. I think before Bessie, maybe.

381.t: Atlantic Records beginnings and his failed push for a black-owned label
381.s: He tried to become a producer and to get Mickey Baker and others to start their own record company.
381.q: I tried to get a job as a producer, you know, behind this, but it never materialized, so I guess, like a lot of people think, playing musicians can't be producers because we don't think like producers, see.

566.t: Contemporary Records and Lester Koenig's lack of promotion
566.s: Humes loved Contemporary and Mr. Koenig but says he never pushed the records beyond sending copies to disc jockeys. She thinks they were her best work; Nat Hentoff and Koenig wrote notes, and Previn, Marty Paich and Wynton Kelly played.
566.q: Once they were made he didn't try to push them. He would just send them to some of the disc jockeys, and if they licked them they'd play them. But he never pushed them at all.

418.t: Luck of recording and the lack of names on records
418.s: Whether you got on a record was luck, and early records did not list the sidemen.
418.ch: Small groups, Europe and Kansas City memories (repeated passages)
418.q: Well, they put it on the folder, but when you get to the record -- suppose the folder gets lost. You got a record you don't know who played what. You know.
